strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question: exploiting the complementarity of vision-only foundation models (VFMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) in transductive zero-shot classification, a setting where few works have explored multi-model integration.

The proposed framework is training-free, lightweight, and model-agnostic, operating entirely in label-probability space, which makes it practical for resource-constrained deployment and plausibly composable with existing transductive methods (e.g., as a pseudo-label generator for Lafter/CPL).

Broad empirical evaluation: 11 standard zero-shot benchmarks, two CLIP backbones (ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50), comparison against many recent training-free and training-based baselines, plus ablations on distribution sources, fusion strategies, joint learning, hyperparameter sensitivity, and convergence.

The reported numbers are strong in absolute terms (e.g., +31.44 on Eurosat, +18.19 on Flowers102 over CLIP ViT-B/16), and the ablation clearly demonstrates that the GMM-visual component (DINOv2-only: 74.20 vs. CLIP 65.24) carries most of the improvement, which is informative.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging the lack of dynamic weighting across VFMs and potential scalability issues.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not clearly validated by the paper's own evidence: in Table 2, naive feature concatenation achieves 75.54% average, exceeding the proposed OTFusion (74.95%). Thus the headline method (distribution fusion via OT) underperforms the simplest fusion baseline, weakening the claim that Optimal Transport fusion is the key mechanism.

The comparison against prior work is potentially unfair: OTFusion uses an additional, much larger VFM (DINOv2 ViT-L/14) alongside CLIP, while all baselines use CLIP alone. Much of the ~10% gain is attributable to adding DINOv2 (DINOv2-only already reaches 74.20%, i.e., +8.96 over CLIP), with OT fusion over CLIP adding only ~0.75%. A fairer comparison would give baselines equivalent access to auxiliary models or report gains attributable specifically to the fusion mechanism.

Technical presentation of the OT formulation has inconsistencies that undermine confidence: Q is defined in R^{N×K} (and Y in R^{N×K} in Algorithm 1) while P and Y are elsewhere R^{N×C}; 'K' and 'C' are used interchangeably. Also, the 'transport' here is essentially Sinkhorn normalization of the element-wise sum of probability matrices (Tr(Q^T P) is an entry-wise agreement term, not a standard transport cost between distributions), so the OT framing is looser than claimed.

Internal contradictions and reproducibility concerns: the implementation sets λ = 0.8, but the sensitivity analysis states performance drops when λ > 0.7; baseline CLIP numbers differ between Table 1 (e.g., 64.78 average) and Table 2 (65.24), with per-dataset discrepancies (e.g., DTD 45.04 vs. 43.50), and the evaluation protocol for these differences is not explained; mixture weights π_c and the number of Sinkhorn iterations are not specified. Code is not yet released.

The Sinkhorn marginal constraints enforce uniform class proportions (Q 1_K = 1_N, Q^T 1_N = 1_K), which is a strong and potentially harmful prior for class-imbalanced test sets; this assumption and its effect are not analyzed.

The 'novel perspective' claim ('first work to systematically investigate VFM/VLM complementarity in transductive ZSL') is overstated; TransCLIP already uses GMM-based transduction, and DINO-assisted prompt learning (Imam et al. 2024) explicitly combines these model families, so the incremental novelty over existing transductive GMM/label-propagation pipelines should be more carefully positioned.

Some claims are imprecise: the text says keeping ε small avoids 'overly uniform predictions' but small ε sharpens (not smooths) transport plans; the citation to Caron et al. 2020 for this choice appears misplaced; the optimization section says the procedure for Eq. (6) 'can be readily extended to the more general objective in Eq. (4)', reversing the general/specific relationship.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question: how to combine complementary strengths of VFMs (DINOv2) and VLMs (CLIP) for transductive zero-shot classification, and the motivation is well illustrated with t-SNE visualizations.

The proposed framework is training-free, lightweight, and operates purely in probability space, which makes it model-agnostic and potentially easy to combine with existing adaptation methods (e.g., as a pseudo-label generator for Lafter/CPL).

Evaluation breadth is good: 11 standard benchmarks, two CLIP backbones (ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50), ablations of distribution sources and fusion strategies, hyperparameter sensitivity, and convergence analysis.
Reported gains are large (average +10% over CLIP), and the ablation isolates the contributions of the semantic prior, the visual GMM prior, and the joint alternating optimization.
weaknesses: Fundamentally unfair comparison protocol. The baselines in Table 1 all use only CLIP, while OTFusion additionally uses DINOv2 ViT-L/14 — a substantially larger, extra model. The headline '+10% over CLIP' therefore mostly reflects the addition of a stronger visual encoder, not the fusion mechanism. The ablation confirms this: DINOv2-only alone reaches 74.20 average vs. 74.95 for the full OTFusion, so nearly the entire gain comes from DINOv2 features. A fair comparison should include baselines that also exploit additional foundation models (e.g., Imam et al. 2024, or simply DINOv2+CLIP ensembles), but no such baselines are reported.

The core methodological claim is undermined by the paper's own ablation: naive feature concatenation (75.54%) outperforms the proposed OT distribution fusion (74.95%). The paper concedes concatenation 'performs well' and argues OT fusion is advantageous for 'scalability and compatibility,' but this significantly weakens the justification for the OT machinery, which is the paper's central contribution.

The transductive Sinkhorn marginal constraint (Q^T 1_N = 1_K) implicitly assumes perfectly class-balanced test sets (each class receives exactly N/K mass). Many of the benchmarks are imbalanced; the impact of this assumption and any class-balance correction is never discussed or analyzed, which is a material methodological gap for a transductive method.

Baseline numbers are internally inconsistent between Table 1 and Table 2: e.g., CLIP on SUN397 is 65.63 in Table 1 but 62.50 ('native CLIP') in Table 2; Aircraft 23.22 vs. 24.70; Eurosat 50.42 vs. 48.30; Food101 82.86 vs. 85.90. It is unclear which protocol produces which numbers, casting doubt on the experimental rigor.

The formulation and presentation have notable technical sloppiness: the abstract/introduction describe 'minimizing transport cost' while Eq. (4) is a maximization; Tr(Q^T P) uses predicted probabilities as transport 'costs,' which is unconventional and weakly connected to actual optimal transport theory; the notation overloads K as both the number of classes and the Sinkhorn kernel matrix; Eqs. (9)-(10) dimensional roles of u and v are confusing; features are inconsistently denoted v_i vs. z_i; Eq. (2) mixes p(v) and N(z; ...). These errors should have been caught.

The claimed novelty ('first work to systematically investigate the complementary strengths of VFMs and VLMs in transductive ZSL') is overclaimed. Combining DINO-family features with CLIP for zero-shot recognition has been explored (e.g., Sus-X uses DINOv1, Imam et al. 2024 which the paper itself discusses), and the GMM-with-shared-covariance component is directly adopted from TransCLIP (Zanella et al. 2024). The incremental novelty over TransCLIP + DINOv2 features + Sinkhorn balancing is modest.

Several reported gains are dominated by datasets where a clustering-based method with DINOv2 features trivially excels (Eurosat +31/+38 points, Flowers102 +18), inflating the average; on fine-grained datasets like Aircraft, OTFusion actually underperforms DMN and even the simple concatenation variant, which is downplayed in the text.

Reproducibility concerns: code is only promised after acceptance; several important details are missing (number of Sinkhorn inner iterations, GMM initialization specifics given the semantic initialization, number of GMM components vs. classes, treatment of the 'number of iterations T').

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: broken citation strings in the references (e.g., 'Jia Deng, R. S. L.-J. L. K. L., Wei Dong', 'MParkhi', 'Subhransu Maji, J. K. M. B.'), typos ('Flowers12', 'Y-only) leads'), a small and hard-to-read Figure 1 with four t-SNE panels that only qualitatively support the claims, and inconsistent result formatting in Table 2 (deltas without superscripts).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: 11 standard zero-shot benchmarks, two CLIP backbones (ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50), comparison against a broad set of recent training-free and training-based methods (TransCLIP, ECALP, TDA, DMN, etc.), with reported absolute numbers that allow verification.

The framework is training-free, model-agnostic in probability space, and positions itself as a plug-and-play pseudo-label enhancer for existing transductive methods, which is practically appealing for low-resource deployment.

Thorough additional analyses: component ablations (Y-only, CLIP-only, DINOv2-only, concatenation, no joint-learning), hyperparameter sensitivity for the entropy regularization and fusion coefficients, and convergence curves showing stable behavior within a few iterations.
The motivation is clearly articulated, supported by t-SNE visualizations of CLIP vs. DINOv2 feature spaces, and the paper is generally well organized and easy to follow.
The alternating optimization (Sinkhorn update for Q interleaved with GMM EM-style updates) is simple, cheap, and the algorithm is fully specified (Algorithm 1), aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central methodological claim is not supported by the paper's own ablation. In Table 2, DINOv2-only already achieves 74.20% average vs. 74.95% for the full OTFusion, and simple feature concatenation reaches 75.54%, i.e., better than the proposed distribution fusion. Thus the vast majority of the +10% headline gain comes from adding a (larger) DINOv2 model and GMM clustering, while the OT fusion machinery—the paper's core contribution—adds ~0.7% over DINOv2-only and is actually inferior to naive concatenation. The text's claim that distribution fusion achieves 'comparable or better results' than concatenation contradicts the reported numbers.

Unfair comparison protocol: all baselines in Table 1 use only CLIP, while OTFusion additionally consumes DINOv2 ViT-L/14 features. The comparison to TransCLIP, ECALP, TDA, and DMN therefore conflates 'better fusion' with 'more/bigger models.' Fairness would require either DINOv2-augmented baselines or at minimum an explicit parameter/compute-matched discussion, which is absent. The most related method (Imam et al. 2024, CLIP meets DINO) is cited but never empirically compared on the same benchmarks.

The Optimal Transport framing appears overstated. Tr(Q^T P) + Tr(Q^T Y) with P, Y being N×C posterior matrices is not a transport cost between two distributions in the standard OT sense; the Sinkhorn step is essentially entropy-regularized doubly-stochastic normalization of a summed similarity matrix, closely resembling assignment/label-propagation components of TransCLIP/ECALP. No theoretical analysis (e.g., convergence of the alternating scheme, properties of the fixed point) is provided, and Fig. 3's 'loss' increasing during a maximization procedure is confusingly described.

The doubly stochastic constraint imposes a balanced-class marginal assumption on the test set, which is a strong and possibly unjustified transductive prior for datasets with non-uniform class distributions; this is not discussed or ablated.

Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers: Table 1's CLIP baseline differs from Table 2's 'native CLIP' (e.g., ImageNet 66.73 vs. 66.60; Flowers102 66.99 vs. 70.70; Pets 86.92 vs. 89.10) without explanation, raising concerns about experimental bookkeeping. The exceptionally large gains on Eurosat (+31.44/+38.21) deserve closer scrutiny (e.g., GMM initialization diagnostics) given they dominate the average.

Notation and presentation sloppiness: K is used both for the number of VFMs and the number of classes (Q ∈ R^{N×K} vs. Y ∈ R^{N×C}); Eq. (12) implies full per-class covariances while the text specifies a shared diagonal covariance; citation formatting is garbled in several places (e.g., 'Manli et al. 2022' for TPT's authors, 'MParkhi et al. 2012').

The claimed novelty ('first work to systematically investigate complementary strengths of VFMs and VLMs in transductive ZSL') is overstated given prior VFM+VLM integration work (Imam et al. 2024; Zhang and Tan 2025) and the close relation of the GMM+Sinkhorn pipeline to existing transductive CLIP methods.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely under-explored problem: training-free integration of heterogeneous foundation models (VFMs and VLMs) for zero-shot classification, motivated by clear observations (Fig. 1) that VLM visual features cluster poorly on fine-grained datasets while VFMs lack semantic alignment.

The proposed formulation is technically sound: squared inner products in the OT objective induce implicit adaptive weighting (λ_v = 2⟨T,P_v⟩), and the MM-based alternating optimization with Sinkhorn updates is derived cleanly in the supplementary, with a non-decreasing objective argument and convergence analysis (Fig. 5).

The evaluation breadth is a major strength: 26 benchmarks spanning natural images, remote sensing, and medical pathology, with reported gains that are large in several domains (e.g., +17.0 over T-CLIP baseline average on remote sensing, 83.9 vs. 76.0 for T-MUSK on medical pathology).

Ablations (Fig. 4, Table 5, Table 7) cover each component: VFM usage, self-adaptive vs. fixed weighting, joint vs. disjoint GMM learning, and model subsets. Table 6 also shows the method outperforms naive max/mean ensembling and adaptive baselines applied per-model, partially mitigating the concern that gains come purely from ensembling.

The framework requires only model outputs (logits/features), not weights, making it applicable to black-box/API-only models, and the computational analysis (Table 6) shows reasonable time/memory relative to graph-based alternatives like ECALP.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is the central concern: SOTA uses much stronger visual encoders (DINOv2 ViT-L/14, DINOv3 ViT-L/16) than all competitors, which operate on CLIP-scale backbones (ViT-B/16, RN50). A large share of the gains (e.g., EuroSAT jumping from ~48 to ~87) plausibly stems from the quality of DINOv3 features rather than the integration mechanism itself. Crucially, there is no baseline that gives competitors access to DINO features (e.g., TransCLIP/GTA-CLIP with CLIP+DINO concatenated features, or a simple weighted logit ensemble with CLIP+DINO) on the natural-image benchmarks. Notably, in Table 1/Table 4 with CLIP-only models (CLIP-1+CLIP-2), SOTA (72.5/71.5) falls below GTA-CLIP (74.5) and COSMIC (73.3), which suggests the core contribution on the standard benchmark is weaker than the headline numbers imply.

The inductive-setting comparison (Table 4) is not apples-to-apples: SOTA fits GMM parameters on the entire unlabeled training set D_u, whereas the starred TTA baselines adapt online from the test stream. Comparing batch-transductive adaptation to streaming TTA overstates the method's relative advantage.

Several methodological details are under-specified: the GMM component-to-class correspondence is never established (GMM on DINO features yields unsupervised clusters; how clusters are associated with class names/text embeddings for the semantic coupling in Eq. (8) is unclear), initialization of Θ is not described, the temperature τ in Eq. (4) is not given, and 'prior-free' claims deserve scrutiny since uniform marginals and GMM over exactly K components encode assumptions about class balance.

Results are not uniformly positive: on Aircraft, SOTA drops below the raw CLIP baseline (22.6 vs. 24.7 transductive; 21.8 inductive), and on DTD it lags ADAPT and GTA-CLIP. These failure cases are not analyzed.

The novelty claim ('first work to systematically investigate complementary strengths of foundation models in zero-shot classification') is overclaimed; multi-model and multi-view ensembling, multi-view clustering, and OT-based fusion all have established literatures, and the delta over prior OT-based transduction (e.g., TransCLIP, which the method closely builds on) is the squared-objective/MM weighting trick — elegant but incremental.

Reproducibility is weakened: the code URL is left empty ('The implementation code is available at:'), some hyperparameter details (τ, Sinkhorn iterations, GMM covariance type in main experiments) are missing from the main paper, and results for several baselines are copied from secondary sources [8, 60] rather than re-run.

Presentation issues: the method name 'SOTA' invites confusion with the abbreviation for state-of-the-art (e.g., 'SOTA: ... achieving SOTA results' would be ambiguous); Table 7's checkmark layout is hard to parse; and the medical Table 5 ablation shows the self-adaptive mechanism yields only +1.3 average, so its practical value is modest despite the framing.

strengths: Breadth of empirical evaluation is a genuine strength: 26 benchmarks spanning natural images, remote sensing, and medical pathology, with comparisons to recent transductive/TTA methods (TransCLIP, ECALP, ADAPT, COSMIC, DMN, etc.).

The optimization procedure is, on paper, technically coherent: the MM derivation in Appendix 6.1 (tangent minorization of the squared terms, Sinkhorn updates for the T-subproblem, EM-style GMM updates) is a valid scheme, and the convergence analysis (Fig. 5) plus the computational complexity discussion (Appendix 8.3, Table 6) address practicality.

The framing that VFMs (DINOv2/v3) provide discriminative visual structure that can correct VLM logits is well motivated and supported by Fig. 1, Fig. 6 (clustering accuracy vs. zero-shot accuracy), and the t-SNE analysis in Fig. 7.
Training-free operation on black-box/API-only models is a practically useful property, and the model-subset analysis (Table 7) shows gains are not tied to one specific backbone combination.
Ablations cover the main design decisions (VFM introduction, self-adaptive weighting, joint vs. disjoint GMM/OT learning) and are reported across all three domains.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. After peeling back the OT language, the core idea is a convex combination of per-model probability matrices whose weights are proportional to agreement with the consensus plan (λ_v = 2⟨T, P_v⟩ in Eq. 13). This is a self-reinforcing consensus/majority-vote weighting scheme; the entropic-OT machinery and the MM iteration largely re-derive a weighted average. The claim that this is 'the first work to systematically investigate the complementary strengths of different foundation models' is overstated — multi-model ensembling, and specifically combining DINO-type visual features with CLIP logits, already appears in works like COSMIC [13], and the OT-for-ensembling idea is incremental relative to [59], which the authors themselves acknowledge as an inspiration.

Concerns about fairness of the headline comparisons. In Table 1 and Table 4, all baselines (GDA, ZLaP, TransCLIP-2, ECALP, ADAPT, GTA-CLIP, COSMIC, DMN, DPE...) operate on a single CLIP backbone, whereas SOTA consumes CLIP plus ViT-L DINOv2/v3 features — a far stronger visual encoder. The +12.6 average gain therefore conflates backbone capacity with the proposed fusion mechanism. The fairer comparisons in Tables 2 and 3 (TransCLIP applied per model, then ensembled, vs. SOTA) show smaller margins, and in Table 4 SOTA with CLIP-only backbones (71.5) actually loses to COSMIC (73.3). The paper's central 'substantial improvements over the best single model' narrative should be established against baselines given the same multi-model inputs, and this is not done for natural images.

Several technical details are underspecified, undermining reproducibility and raising questions about the method's robustness. (i) The class marginal q ∈ Δ^K is never defined — presumably uniform, which hard-codes a balanced-class assumption that is unrealistic for many datasets and unstated. (ii) The GMM initialization, which strongly determines the fixed point of the joint optimization, is not described (does it use CLIP pseudolabels? random? k-means?). (iii) The number of Sinkhorn iterations, convergence tolerance, and sensitivity to ϵ and τ are not analyzed. (iv) Appendix notation contradicts the main text: p ∈ Δ^N (samples) in Sec. 3.1 becomes p ∈ R^K and q ∈ R^N in Eqs. (17)-(18); the denominator Q_ic in Eq. (19) is undefined; Eq. (20) omits the per-component index. The code link in the abstract is empty.

The 'self-adaptive' mechanism has a rich-get-richer bias that the paper does not confront. Since λ_v ∝ ⟨T, P_v⟩, models that agree with the current plan gain weight, suppressing diversity exactly when it is most needed; the ablation (Fig. 4, +0.2/+0.3/+0.8 for self-adaptive vs. non-adaptive) shows the effect is marginal in practice, and the authors' own explanation for the modest gain is hand-wavy.

There are non-trivial failure cases that go unexplained: SOTA with CLIP-1+CLIP-2 degrades Aircraft by −2.1 points relative to raw CLIP-1 (Table 1, Table 4), and several individual datasets show regressions, yet no analysis of when/why the ensemble hurts is provided.

Maximizing a sum of convex quadratic terms ⟨T,P_v⟩² over the transport polytope is not a concave program; the MM scheme is only guaranteed to reach a stationary point, and with the undisclosed initialization the procedure could land in poor local optima. The convergence claim ('converges to a stationary point') is accurate but is presented more favorably than it deserves.
No statistical rigor: results are single-run point estimates on a stochastic method (GMM fitting, initialization), with no variance, seeds, or significance testing.

Presentation issues accumulate: the abstract's code link is blank, dataset name inconsistencies (WSSS4LUAD/WSSS4LUDA/WSSS4LUDA), Eq. (2)'s entropy convention, and Table 6's odd 'Vanilla(max/mean)' rows suggest the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and under-explored question: integrating complementary strengths of VFMs and VLMs for zero-shot classification, rather than improving a single model.

The proposed method is training-free, requires only model outputs (compatible with API-only black-box models), and uses an MM-based alternating optimization that is well-motivated and clearly derived in the supplementary material (Algorithm 1, with the tangent minorization leading to self-adaptive weights).

Evaluation breadth is a clear strength: 26 benchmarks spanning natural images, remote sensing, and medical pathology, with substantial reported gains (e.g., +17.0 average on remote sensing over the best single model in Table 2, +14.1 on medical in Table 3).

Ablations cover the main components (VFM introduction, self-adaptive weighting vs. fixed weights, joint vs. disjoint learning), and the model-subset analysis (Table 7) shows consistent gains across different model combinations, supporting robustness of the ensemble mechanism.
Convergence analysis (Fig. 5) and computational efficiency comparison (Table 6) indicate the method is practical, running in under ~1 second with modest memory.
The paper is generally well written, with a clear problem formulation, related-work positioning, and reproducibility details (models, epsilon, initialization, hardware).
weaknesses: The comparison is not fully fair: SOTA's strongest results rely on pairing ViT-B/16-scale VLMs with much larger visual encoders (DINOv2 ViT-L/14, DINOv3 ViT-L/16), while baseline methods (GTA-CLIP, ADAPT, TransCLIP, ECALP, DMN, COSMIC) appear to operate on ViT-B/16-scale features only. A large portion of the gain may thus stem from using stronger/more expensive visual features rather than from the proposed self-adaptive OT ensemble itself. Applying TransCLIP/ADAPT to DINOv3 features would be an essential control.

On the only configuration where SOTA uses matched-scale models (CLIP-1+CLIP-2, Table 1), the average accuracy (72.5) is below GTA-CLIP (74.5) and below ADAPT on several datasets, and even regresses relative to CLIP-1 on Aircraft (22.6 vs. 24.7). This weakens the claim that the ensemble mechanism itself is the main driver.

The squared objective (Eq. 7) is ad hoc. Squaring ⟨T, P_v⟩ makes model weights proportional to both alignment quality and the absolute magnitude of the probability matrices, which are incomparable across models due to different softmax temperatures (Eq. 4) and GMM posterior sharpness. No sensitivity analysis or theoretical justification for this specific nonlinearity is provided; other concave/convex transformations are not compared.

The role of the target marginal q is not discussed. A fixed (presumably uniform) class marginal bakes in a class-balanced prior over the test set, which is a known transductive assumption that can fail on imbalanced test sets; this somewhat conflicts with the 'prior-free' claim and should be analyzed.

There is a label-correspondence ambiguity that is glossed over: GMM components (Eq. 3) are unlabeled, so the posterior over mixture components must somehow be aligned to the K semantic classes. The paper does not explain how this permutation/alignment is resolved (presumably implicitly via the joint optimization with VLM posteriors), which affects both clarity and correctness of the transductive solution.

The claimed novelty ('first work to systematically investigate complementary strengths of different foundation models in zero-shot classification') is overstated; ensembling multiple VLM outputs is a known strategy (e.g., multi-encoder CLIP ensembles, max/mean fusion baselines in Table 6), so the incremental novelty over prior ensemble + transduction work (e.g., TransCLIP) should be stated more carefully.

The self-adaptive mechanism's benefit is small in the aggregate ablation (+0.2 to +1.4 in Fig. 4), and the authors' own explanation concedes this; the more striking gains come from introducing VFMs, so the central methodological contribution (self-adaptive OT) is supported by relatively modest evidence.

Code availability is claimed in the abstract but the URL is empty, and several experimental details (e.g., which DINO/GMM covariance settings, exact prompt templates, hyperparameters for the medical/remote-sensing runs) are deferred to code, limiting reproducibility of the reported tables as-is.
